item.title: 1958: Bob Turley Wins Cy Young Award, Edging Warren Spahn
item.description: New York Yankees pitcher Bob Turley, who posted a 21–7 record with 168 strikeouts and a 2.97 earned run average, wins the Cy Young Award. With only one award given for the two leagues, Turley gathers five votes to four for the previous winner, Warren Spahn of the Milwaukee Braves, who went 22–11 with 150 strikeouts and a 3.07 ERA. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 2023: Young Leaves Braves to Join Angels as Third Base Coach
item.description: On November 12, 2023, Young confirmed that he would be leaving the Braves to join the Los Angeles Angels coaching staff as their new third base coach under newly appointed manager Ron Washington. Photo: All-Pro Reels from District of Columbia, USA (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2020: Jose Abreu, Freddie Freeman Win MLB MVP Awards
item.description: Jose Abreu of the Chicago White Sox and Freddie Freeman of the Atlanta Braves Respectively win the MLB MVP Awards. Photo: TonyTheTiger (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2020: Hoffman Retires From Coaching, Joins Padres Front Office
item.description: On November 12, 2020, Hoffman retired from coaching and began working for the Padres front office in an advisory role. Photo: Adam Moss from East Amherst, New York, United States (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2019: Giants Hire Gabe Kapler to Replace Retiring Bruce Bochy
item.description: The San Francisco Giants hire Gabe Kapler who previously managed the Philadelphia Phillies but was fired at the end of last season as the new manager replacing Bruce Bochy who retired at the end of last season. Photo: Johnmaxmena2 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2014: Kluber, Kershaw Win American League and National League Cy Young
item.description: Corey Kluber of the Cleveland Indians and Clayton Kershaw of the Los Angeles Dodgers earn the Cy Young Award in the American League and National League, respectively. Photo: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2014: Ballpark Digest Reports Lancaster JetHawks Being Sold
item.description: On November 12, 2014, Ballpark Digest reported that the Lancaster JetHawks were being sold by Peter A.

item.title: 2006: Ramirez Signs Five-Year Deal With Cubs
item.description: On November 12, 2006, Ramírez signed a five-year deal with the Cubs. Photo: Jauerback (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 2004: Garms Inducted Into Texas Baseball Hall of Fame
item.description: On November 12, 2004, Garms was inducted into the Texas Baseball Hall of Fame alongside Kenny Rogers, Rube Foster, Craig Biggio, Jeff Bagwell, Bill Brown and Jim Gilligan at the J.

item.title: 2002: Miguel Tejada Named American League MVP With 21 First-Place Votes
item.description: Oakland Athletics shortstop Miguel Tejada, who receives 356 points from the BBWAA, including 21 first-place votes of the 28 cast, is selected as the American League MVP. Tejada joins countrymen George Bell (1987) and Sammy Sosa (1998) as Dominican Republic natives to win the award. Photo: dbking on Flickr (Original version) UCinternational (Crop) (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1998: Joe Torre Named American League Manager of the Year
item.description: In an unforgettable season, Joe Torre was named the American League Manager of the Year for the 2nd time in 3 years. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 1997: Ken Griffey Jr. Unanimous Pick for American League MVP
item.description: Ken Griffey Jr. of the Seattle Mariners becomes the ninth unanimous pick for the American League MVP Award. Griffey hit .304 for Seattle, led the AL with 56 home runs, and led the Majors with 147 RBI. He receives all 28 first-place votes and 392 points in balloting to become the first unanimous AL pick since Frank Thomas in 1993, and the 13th unanimous selection overall. Photo: Keith Allison (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 1996: Pat Hentgen Edges Andy Pettitte for American League Cy Young
item.description: Pat Hentgen of the Toronto Blue Jays edges Andy Pettitte of the New York Yankees for the Cy Young Award in the closest American League voting since 1972 when Gaylord Perry tops Wilbur Wood by six points. Hentgen, who posts a 20-10 record with a 3.22 ERA and leads the Major Leagues in complete games (10), outpoints Pettitte (21-8, 3.87) by the narrow margin of 110-104. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0).

item.title: 1993: Bill Dickey, 86, Hall of Fame Catcher for New York Yankees
item.description: Bill Dickey, 86, Hall of Fame and 11-time All-Star catcher for the New York Yankees over 17 seasons spanning 1928–1946, who posted a lifetime batting average of .313 with 202 home runs and 1,209 RBI and was a member of seven World Series champion teams; set a record by catching 100 or more games in 13 straight seasons while holding a World Series record for catching games (38); reached double digits in home runs… Photo: Harris & Ewing (Public domain).

item.title: 1992: Arbitrator Overturns Lifetime Ban of Yankees Pitcher Steve Howe
item.description: Arbitrator George Nicolau overturns the lifetime ban of New York Yankees pitcher Steve Howe for substance abuse, considering it too severe. After that, Howe is re-signed by the team.

item.title: 1982: Joe Altobelli Named Orioles Manager, Succeeding Earl Weaver
item.description: Joe Altobelli, former manager of the San Francisco Giants (1977–1979), is named Earl Weaver's successor to pilot the Baltimore Orioles. Altobelli, 50, is no stranger to the Orioles; he was the highly successful skipper of their Triple-A Rochester Red Wings farm team before taking the Giants' job. Photo: kc congdon from rochester, ny (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1975: Tom Seaver Wins Third Cy Young Award With Mets
item.description: Tom Seaver of the New York Mets wins his third Cy Young Award, after led the National League pitchers with 22 victories and 243 strikeouts while posting a 2.38 ERA. Seaver had previously won the award in 1969 and 1973. Photo: slgckgc (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1969: Harmon Killebrew Named American League MVP With 49 Homers
item.description: Harmon Killebrew of the Minnesota Twins is voted the American League's Most Valuable Player after he led the league with 49 home runs, 140 RBI, and a .430 on-base percentage. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1966: Dodgers Complete 18-Game Japan Tour With 9-8-1 Record
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers complete an 18-game tour of Japan with a 9–8–1 record. The eight losses are the most for an MLB club touring the Far East.

item.title: 1959: Nellie Fox Wins American League MVP With 295 Points
item.description: Nellie Fox of the Chicago White Sox wins the American League MVP Award with 295 points. Teammates Luis Aparicio (255) and Early Wynn (123) finish second and third respectively. Photo: Kilpatrick (Public domain).

item.title: 1957: Frank Lane Resigns as Cardinals GM, Joins Cleveland Indians
item.description: "Trader" Frank Lane resigns as general manager of the St. Louis Cardinals and is replaced by Bing Devine. Lane, 62, is then hired to succeed Hank Greenberg as GM of the Cleveland Indians, where he will enhance his reputation as a compulsive wheeler-dealer through the end of the 1960 season.

item.title: 1956: Mickey Mantle Unanimous Winner of American League MVP
item.description: Triple-Crown winner and World Series champion Mickey Mantle is the unanimous winner of the 1956 American League Most Valuable Player Award with 24 out of 24 first-place votes. Eight days later, 27-game-winner Don Newcombe garners 66 percent of the votes to take the National League Most Valuable Player Award; fellow Dodger pitcher Sal Maglie, with 54%, runs second. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1955: Fred Hutchinson, 36, Takes Over Cardinals as Manager
item.description: Former Detroit Tigers pitcher and manager Fred Hutchinson, 36, replaces Harry Walker at the helm of the St. Louis Cardinals. With the departure of Walker, 1956 will be the first year in the National League's 80-year history without a player-manager.

item.title: 1952: Bobby Shantz Wins AL MVP After 24-7 Season
item.description: Bobby Shantz, who posted a 24–7 record with 152 strikeouts and a 2.48 ERA for the Philadelphia Athletics, is selected the American League Most Valuable Player by the Baseball Writers' Association of America and the AL Pitcher of the Year by The Sporting News.

item.title: 1947: Browns Draft Garvin Hamner, Brother of Granny Hamner
item.description: The St. Louis Browns select second baseman Garvin Hamner from Memphis of the Double-A Southern Association in the minor league draft. Garvin is the elder brother of Philadelphia Phillies' prospect Granny Hamner, a future three-time NL All-Star, and reports at the time claim the Browns mistook the two Hamners, and drafted the wrong brother. A St. Louis spokesman denies the charge.

item.title: 1940: Roger Peckinpaugh, 49, Returns to Manage Cleveland Indians
item.description: Roger Peckinpaugh gets a second chance to manage the Cleveland Indians, signing a two-year contract to return to the team that fired him on June 8, 1933. The 49-year-old ex-shortstop, a Cleveland native, compiled a 415–402 mark during his first term, which lasted 5½ seasons. He takes over a dissension-riddled club that openly rebelled against ex-skipper Ossie Vitt, yet finished second in 1940. Photo: Bain News Service, publisher (Public domain).

item.title: 1923: Giants Trade Casey Stengel, Dave Bancroft to Boston Braves
item.description: New York Giants owner and manager John McGraw trades outfielders Casey Stengel and Bill Cunningham along with shortstop Dave Bancroft to the Boston Braves in exchange for pitchers Joe Oeschger and Bill Southworth. Photo: The Library of Congress (Public domain).

item.title: 1920: Owners Elect Kenesaw Mountain Landis Sole Commissioner
item.description: MLB owners unanimously elect Kenesaw Mountain Landis as sole commissioner of Major League Baseball for seven years, abolishing the National Baseball Commission. The owners' action comes in direct response to the Black Sox Scandal, which threatens the integrity of the game. Landis agreed on the condition that he would be the sole commissioner, with final authority over the players and owners. Photo: Not known. There is a copyright notice, to Underwood and (illegible) (Public domain).

item.title: 1893: Dauvray Cup Last Mentioned in Newport, Kentucky
item.description: According to John Thorn, official historian of Major League Baseball, the last mention of the presence of the Dauvray Cup was on November 12, 1893, in Newport, Kentucky.

item.title: 1886: Browns Trade Hugh Nicol to Red Stockings for Jack Boyle
item.description: The first trade ever of two reserve players takes place as the St. Louis Browns send Hugh Nicol and cash to the Cincinnati Red Stockings for Jack Boyle. Photo: Goodwin & Company (Public domain).
